papers.title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

papers.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
papers.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing me

papers.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
papers.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impa

papers.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
papers.abstract: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls. Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost

papers.title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
papers.abstract: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate t

papers.title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
papers.abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI

papers.title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features,

papers.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
papers.abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and indivi

papers.title: Isabelle Pool Server: a pooled verification service for prover training and multi-agent proving
papers.abstract: Isabelle Pool Server (IPS), a verification service with a pool of warm headless Isabelle sessions behind an HTTP API, with session leasing and reclamation, memory-aware admission control, and a time budget on every call. Its verification interface spans single-step execution, block-level proof checking and whole-theory builds, with checkpoints for cheap branching and backtracking, and a build from scratch as the final arbiter. The service runs as a single container with monitoring and is accessible via a Python client, two MCP servers and a raw HTTP API. In our measurements IPS is level with PIDE MCP, a PIDE frontend for agents, at one worker and ahead of it at eight, at its commit of October 2026 (the tool is now PIDE AI). Once its sessions are up it scales to 32 concurrent workers on one host at 24 times the single-worker rate, and under memory pressure it refuses new sessions rather t

papers.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
papers.abstract: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive

papers.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
papers.abstract: Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change. \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. It preserves the original specification as authoritative ground truth and appends confidence-filtered ref

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of In-Context Learning and Out-of-Context Hallucination
papers.abstract: Large language models can infer and follow specific rules through in-context learning (ICL), yet may fail to remain faithful to provided evidence, giving rise to out-of-context (OOC) hallucination. Existing work has largely investigated the underlying mechanisms of ICL and OOC hallucination along separate lines. However, this separation obscures the mechanistic basis for these seemingly opposing outcomes. In this work, we study this contrast through the unified view of functional roles in dynamic context. The key observation is that role information can be internally represented without reliably constraining output. We derive a first-order decomposition to characterize the role effect, showing that its substantial influence depends on two necessary conditions, namely sufficient contribution magnitude and coherent signed aggregation. Causal analysis further shows that role span contributi

papers.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
papers.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate A

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Acro

papers.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the

papers.title: APS: Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection for Long Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) have significantly improved video understanding capabilities, yet processing long videos remains challenging due to the substantial computational cost of extensive visual inputs. Frame selection offers an efficient alternative, but many existing region-based methods rely on fixed or predefined temporal partitions, which may result in suboptimal temporal regions, compromising subsequent budget allocation and frame selection. In this work, we propose Adaptive Partitioning-Based Frame Selection (APS), a training-free framework that adapts temporal partitions to local variations in query-frame relevance. Specifically, APS formulates temporal partitioning as a complexity-regularized fitting problem, jointly optimizing partition boundaries and local models through dynamic programming. The resulting adaptive temporal partitions guide frame

papers.title: AeroRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow natural-language instructions, yet still fail frequently in closed-loop flight. Correcting these failures requires repairs, i.e., actions that avoid them at the states the policy itself reaches, which human pilots cannot label at scale and rule-based planners cannot supply reliably. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Our key insight is that a failing policy should judge its own repairs by flying on from them. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its sup

papers.title: How Complete Must an Environment Be to Train a Capable GUI Agent?
papers.abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are widely trained in executable GUI environments. To lower cost, build environments in batches, and reduce manual effort, each work trades away part of the environment through its construction choices. We describe these choices along three dimensions: reward coverage, the goal-reaching trajectories the verifier rewards; data coverage, the application data the agent is exposed to beyond what the task reads or writes; and feature coverage, the application features beyond what the task uses. Existing works set each dimension on engineering grounds, but they do not measure its effect on training. How complete must an environment be to train a capable agent, and along which dimensions? In MobileGym, we adjust each dimension separately, train Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, and evaluate every policy in the original full environment. A verifier that rewards only one

papers.title: Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams
papers.abstract: Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.

papers.title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

papers.title: Interpreting Timestamp Permutations in Dynamic Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Timestamp permutations are used to test whether dynamic link predictors exploit temporal information, but a performance gap can reflect changes in training, evaluation history, or both. We separate these effects with a crossed diagnostic and measure input exposure: whether altered histories actually change the predictor's inputs. On MOOC, TCL trained with binary cross-entropy gains approximately eight pairwise-accuracy points from original-chronology training under either evaluation history, while changing history at fixed weights gives only 0.03 points. The small history contrast reflects unchanged inputs for 68.37% of queries, stable rankings for most others, and cancellation of gains and losses. Under original evaluation history, suppressing explicit time encoding reduces the training contrast from 8.03 to 3.64 points, a paired reduction of 4.39 points (95% interval [3.68, 5.09]) acro

papers.title: Inherited Adapter Experts for Replay-Free Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each exper

papers.title: PhysDial: Adapting Pretrained Video Models for PDE Simulation under Changing Physical Conditions
papers.abstract: Simulating how physical systems respond to changing conditions is central to control, design, and scenario studies. To our knowledge, prior PDE foundation models have not been trained or evaluated on changes within trajectories. Our counterfactual test measures how far predictions move toward a changed solver branch from the same state. Models trained on fixed conditions follow changes only partly. A PDE foundation model given a condition input after pretraining barely responds. PhysDial adapts a pretrained video diffusion transformer to eight two-dimensional PDE families. Coefficients enter with the noise level, condition fields as reference frames, and equation text as a prompt. In Kolmogorov flow, switches within trajectories account for about 5% of the training samples. At matched compute, they halve the error after a change in forcing wavenumber or amplitude. A few trajectories at n

papers.title: LEDGE: An Efficient Simulator for Distributed LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Devices
papers.abstract: Evaluating distributed large language model (LLM) serving on heterogeneous edge devices requires exploring diverse model partitions, device placements, and network conditions, making repeated physical experiments costly. An efficient simulator for edge LLM serving must support diverse, fine-grained placement configurations, capture runtime behavior, and accurately predict execution times while keeping simulation overhead low. We present LEDGE, a lightweight simulator for fast, fine-grained evaluation of distributed LLM serving on heterogeneous edge devices without executing tensor operations. LEDGE constructs event graphs supporting non-uniform tensor and pipeline parallelism, estimates execution costs using reusable performance models calibrated from end-to-end measurements, and simulates shared-link contention. We evaluate LEDGE on a heterogeneous testbed of 10 Jetson and Raspberry Pi

papers.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verifica

papers.title: SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification
papers.abstract: The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to pr

papers.title: Measuring What Matters in the Age of AI: The Research Software Metrics Landscape
papers.abstract: Research software now serves as a primary instrument of science, but the methods the community uses to judge its quality, sustainability, reuse, and impact remain scattered across software engineering, open science, FAIR software, citation, and research-assessment literature. AI-assisted development sharpens the problem: code can be produced at rates that outpace human review capacity, provenance and attribution are harder to track, scholarly credit systems cannot keep pace, and existing metrics inherit assumptions about how research software gets developed that may no longer apply. To aid in navigating these challenges, we present a focused landscape synthesis of research software metrics based on 49 substantive references, organizing the recurring metrics into eight families described by data source, claimed construct, evidence of validity, automation potential, and susceptibility to m

papers.title: Ask the Peers: Ranking NFR Coverage Gaps for Requirements Review
papers.abstract: Missing or underrepresented non-functional requirements (NFR) categories leave little direct evidence in a requirements set, making them difficult to identify during requirements review. In this study, we frame NFR coverage-gap review as a project-level ranking task: given a target requirements specification, the goal is to rank the 11 PROMISE NFR categories for analyst inspection. We compare seven statistical, embedding-based, and large language model (LLM)-based configurations that differ in both ranking mechanism and evidence source, including target requirement statements, peer requirements, their semantic representation, and peer category statistics. We evaluate the configurations using controlled gap injection with leave-one-project-out evaluation on PROMISE, PROMISE+, PURE-Transport, and PURE-Business. Four configurations that use peer category statistics are effectively tied unde

papers.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A n

papers.title: Ephyra: A Property-Based Testing Framework for the LLM Era
papers.abstract: Coding agents now write a growing share of software tests; however, property-based testing (PBT) libraries are designed with historical considerations. We present Ephyra, a PBT library in Rust built on three concepts: customizability, observability and generator synthesis. Ephyra lets users compose their own testing loops from generation, mutation and shrinking, and synthesize these components to satisfy functional predicates. Applying Ephyra to 14 open source systems, we have found 349 bugs and reported 300 of them, in database management systems (SQLite, Turso, PostgreSQL, DuckDB, DataFusion), the verified policy engine (Cedar), the SQL equivalence prover (QED), the URL parser used in Node.js (ada-url), reimplementations of existing open source systems in Rust (coreutils, brush, gitoxide), and compilers (binaryen, OCaml, and OxCaml).

papers.title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
papers.abstract: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. papers.title: ProbMedTOD: A Bayesian Network Guided Task-Oriented Dialogue System for Patient History Taking
papers.abstract: Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. Deploying AI in this setting is constrained by privacy, cost, and latency, making Small Language Models (SLMs) a more desirable backbone compared to larger LLMs. However, SLMs capture only the fast, intuitive "System 1" side of this process and lack explicit mechanisms for the deliberative "System 2" reasoning needed to maintain and update diagnostic uncertainty over time. Bayesian Networks (BayesNets) offer a natural complement, providing an interpretable framework for auditable probabilistic belief tracking. Yet, clinical BayesNets are difficult to construct due to their reliance on expert curated structure, dependencies, and parameters. We introduce ProbMedTOD, which automat

papers.title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
papers.abstract: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodologica

papers.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. papers.title: Compression Effects on Low-Resource Multilingual Translation
papers.abstract: We present a pilot study characterising the effect of post-training quantisation on multilingual machine translation quality and inference cost for three African languages - Hausa, Swahili, and Yoruba - across three model families: a small general-purpose LLM (Qwen2.5-1.5B), a larger multilingual instruction-tuned LLM (Aya-23-8B), and a dedicated multilingual MT model (NLLB-200-distilled-1.3B). Evaluating on the FLORES-200 devtest set (1,012 sentences per direction) under FP16, bitsandbytes INT8, and NF4 INT4 precisions on consumer-grade NVIDIA T4 GPUs, we find: (i) the specialised MT model outperforms both LLMs by 32.7-43.3 chrF on the Hausa and Swahili directions, and by 12.9-24.7 chrF on Yoruba, despite being roughly a sixth the size of the 8B instruction-tuned LLM; (ii) post-training quantisation preserves aggregate translation quality within approximately 1 chrF across all model fam

papers.title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
papers.abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of cor

papers.title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
papers.abstract: This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-5-mini both as an independent neural translator and when used within a more complex process that includes self-assessment and improvement. As a standalone model, GPT-5-mini produced very fluent translations , achieving a COMET score of 0.8649 and receiving high human scores for adequacy, fluency, and style (averaging 4.53 out of 5). When used in a system that combined translation with self-assessm

papers.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with

papers.title: DyNA-Mixer: Decoupling Time and Topology for Scalable Dynamic Node Affinity Prediction
papers.abstract: Continuous-time dynamic graphs preserve the ordering, timing, and evolving strength of interactions that static snapshots discard, making dynamic graph mining essential for evolving systems such as recommender systems, trade networks, and transaction platforms. Research in this area has centered on dynamic link prediction, which forecasts only whether a future interaction will occur, whereas many applications also need its intensity. The dynamic node affinity prediction (DNAP) problem generalizes this task to continuous targets and full-candidate ranking, making it more broadly applicable but substantially harder. This raises two coupled difficulties: ranking requires a predictor expressive enough to capture both multi-scale temporal evolution and graph-wide collaborative patterns, yet running such a predictor over every source--destination pair is computationally prohibitive. We propose

papers.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors

papers.title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
papers.abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail s

papers.title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
papers.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. In this paper, we argue that prototypes remain overlooked and underutilized, and should be integrated as a complementary, intuitive gateway to auditing complex machine learning models. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts al

papers.title: Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification for Weather Forecasting: Conformal Prediction Under Spatiotemporal Dependence
papers.abstract: Conformal prediction gives finite-sample, distribution-free marginal coverage and has begun to be applied to gridded weather forecasts. Marginal coverage concerns the long-run fraction of covered points at a location, not how coverage behaves jointly across space and time on a given day. I benchmark eight interval-construction procedures (Gaussian, pooled and per-cell split conformal, per-season, adaptive conformal inference and rolling windows) for gridded 2 m temperature forecasts at eight lead times from 6 hours to 10 days, using ERA5 at 5.625 degree resolution, a deliberately modest convolutional forecaster and ECMWF's operational HRES, with calibration in 2017-2018 and testing in 2019-2021. Alongside coverage, width and interval score, I report dependence diagnostics: a spatial overdispersion index, quantiles of daily spatial coverage and miss persistence relative to a shuffled-days

papers.title: On Evaluating User Simulators for Interactive Agents
papers.abstract: User simulators offer a scalable way to evaluate interactive agents, but how to assess their quality remains underexplored. In particular, it is unclear whether existing user simulator evaluation frameworks reliably detect meaningful failures in simulated user behavior. This uncertainty makes it difficult to interpret simulator evaluation. To understand what a high benchmark score tells us about simulator quality, we (meta-)evaluate the metrics themselves. To instantiate this meta-evaluation, we deliberately perturb simulated replays to induce failures such as altered goals, omitted constraints, premature stopping, and acceptance of broken work, then test whether the metrics penalize these failures. Evaluation methods from three prior studies detect only 5-6 of the 10 perturbations; their combined scores even favor populations instructed to accept broken work over unmodified controls. Mo

papers.title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
papers.abstract: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. A more faithful approximation of operator behavior requires not only accurate state predictions, but also correct variations along local perturbation directions. We present TangentPDE, which uses finite differences to approximate directional derivatives and constructs task-relevant finite-step responses from the state outputs of a reference solver at sparse paired inputs. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. papers.title: Training-free motion statistics match self-supervised behavior encoders
papers.abstract: Self-supervised encoders for animal behavior are often trained on, or fed, hand-built movement features. We ask whether they beat those ingredients when compared fairly. A training-free representation, made of generic per-frame measurements summarized over fixed time windows and reduced with PCA, is compared with retrained and released encoders (BAMS, hBehaveMAE) under a preregistered protocol: frozen representations of equal size and one shared classifier. On CalMS21 it reaches 85.8 macro F1 against 82.4 for the best encoder, ties with four labelled videos, and leads when the annotator changes or new behaviors must be learned from a few videos; the reading holds for encoders retrained with three seeds. On the MABe22 mouse triplets it scores 83.7 against 80.3 for the released hBehaveMAE (gap +3.4, 95% interval +2.1 to +4.7). On a second species, the MABe22 fly groups, the same recipe sco

papers.title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
papers.abstract: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow

papers.title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
papers.abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. papers.title: Beyond Cross-Modal Reconstruction: Participant-Level Evaluation of sEMG-Kinematic Coupling in Post-Stroke Gait
papers.abstract: Accurate cross-modal reconstruction is often treated as evidence of physiological coupling, although it may simply reflect temporal patterns shared across participants. We tested whether frozen bidirectional models captured subject-specific neuromuscular coupling between electromyographic activity and gait kinematics in 82 held-out able-bodied and 43 post-stroke participants. Complete source-modality removal and cross-participant source substitution, along with a cycle-position-age-sex template baseline, were applied. Learned bilateral asymmetry was also compared with transparent waveform and derivative asymmetry for predicting Performance-Oriented Mobility Assessment (POMA) scores in the case of repeated nested cross-validation. papers.title: When Normal-Only Updates Are Not Enough: Test-Time Adaptation in Reconstruction-Based Time-Series Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Normal operating conditions can evolve after deployment, motivating test-time adaptation (TTA) of time-series anomaly detectors using incoming data. Yet the same stream may contain anomalies, so TTA with online updates must decide which test samples should be used for adaptation. This leaves a more basic question: even if updates are restricted to samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, does TTA reliably improve anomaly detection? We study this question with a controlled intervention that replaces the practical update selector with a rule that uses only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark, while keeping the rest of the online adaptation procedure unchanged. Across nine benchmark families, four optimizer configurations, and five random seeds, we obtain three main findings: (1) using only samples labeled as normal in the benchmark does not reliably improve detection; (2) practic

papers.title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
papers.abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. papers.title: VAFL: A Vertical Analytic Federated Learning Mechanism for Efficient Crowdsourced Services via Closed-Form Solutions
papers.abstract: Intelligent services often rely on complementary information held by different organizations, motivating Vertical Federated Learning without centralized raw-data pooling. We propose VAFL, a Vertical Analytic Federated Learning framework that fits classification and regression heads on fixed local representations through regularized least squares. An agent-assisted protected-computation workflow supports two-party and multi-party collaboration. To reduce fitting overhead, we develop a full-dimensional equivalent solve that applies block factors directly to the target matrix, avoiding construction of the full inverse. We further study two width-reduction strategies: local spectral projection with coefficient lifting, and full-dimensional local fitting with low-rank cross-party correction. papers.title: RespCCT and FreqCCT: Compact, Explainable and Cost-Aware Convolutional Transformers for Multi-Class Respiratory Disease Classification
papers.abstract: Chest auscultation depends on the listener, and software that classifies lung sounds could give a second reading where trained listeners are scarce. The most accurate published classifiers fine-tune large pretrained networks, and their accuracy is rarely reported with running cost or paired statistics. This study makes three contributions. (i) It proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers of 173,187 and 124,999 parameters that learn from random initialization on mel, constant-Q and cepstral images of 5 s frames from three public databases, ICBHI, KAUH and RD@TR, with 1,665 audio files in seven classes. (ii) It compares both models with five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants on one test set, using paired bootstrap intervals. (iii) It measures the cost of every pipeline stage on one CPU thread, tests whether attribution maps depend on the

papers.title: What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of survival analysis methods, current benchmarks often operate under narrow conditions: they heavily rely on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, and frequently either exclude deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresent challenging dataset regimes. To address these limitations, we conduct a large-scale, neutral benchmark comparing 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 diverse datasets. Crucially, we treat the model selection criterion (optimizing for C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable. Using Bayesian mixed-effects modeling, we demonstrate that evaluation design heavily dictates conclusions. For complex DL and tree-based architectures, selecting hyperparameters to optimize for IBS instead of C-index yields substantial improvements in probabili

papers.title: DuoCL: Dual-Path Online Continual Learning
papers.abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires learning from a data stream whose arrival rate is independent of model training speed. When training cannot keep pace, computationally expensive gradient-based methods update less frequently, limiting adaptation. Analytic methods reduce this overhead, but their frozen backbones cannot adapt representations to changing distributions. We propose DuoCL, a dual-path OCL framework whose fast analytic path accumulates feature statistics from every incoming minibatch while its slow path periodically adapts the backbone. The slow path adjusts its sample count to the available compute budget without interrupting fast-path learning. Feature alignment compensates for drift in the accumulated classifier statistics. Across four datasets and three computational budgets, DuoCL improves online accuracy by an average of 9.67 percentage points over the strongest gr

papers.title: The geometry of neural network decision boundaries
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are built using well-understood mathematical operations, yet their complex nature poses significant challenges to intuitively understanding their decision-making processes. This work introduces a method for visualizing and measuring ANN decision boundary geometry directly in the high-dimensional input space, avoiding distortions found with traditional projection-based techniques. We analyze boundary curvatures and distances in diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods. Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as the size of the subspace increases, suggesting that decision boundaries are close to input samples within large, continuous subspaces. papers.title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
papers.abstract: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve

papers.title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
papers.abstract: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it. CratesBump is built from every crate on crates.io with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public crates.io data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which

papers.title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. papers.title: JEPA for astronomy: multi-survey spectral alignment puts stellar parameters on the leading principal axes
papers.abstract: Spectra from different surveys carry different systematics and are not calibrated against one another. Multi-survey foundation models for stellar spectra are then built by aligning embeddings of the same star observed across surveys. Most in astronomy follow the recipes established for language and vision, aligning with a contrastive loss that separates every star from the others. However, this does not ensure that the stellar physics is encoded in a form that a simple read-out can recover. Holding the cross-survey architecture fixed and varying only the alignment loss, we measure what an objective encodes from the principal-component geometry of the Gaia BP/RP (XP) spectra and from a linear probe of the stellar parameters. papers.title: A Survey on the Use of Machine Learning within Computer Algebra
papers.abstract: This survey explores the use of Machine Learning (ML) in the field of Computer Algebra (CA), both to optimise existing CA algorithms, and to perform symbolic computation directly. Traditional symbolic methods, while mathematically rigorous, often are computationally expensive thus limiting their use in real-world applications. Recent advances have shown that data-driven techniques can address these limitations by guiding heuristic decisions, selecting optimal algorithms, predicting structural properties of algebraic objects, or even making direct symbolic computations. We take a systematic literature review approach and uncover work in CA applications including cylindrical algebraic decomposition, Gröbner basis computation, symbolic integration, and many more. The survey compares the different ML approaches that have been employed for these tasks, ranging from decision trees to transform

papers.title: Who Changed the AI Agent's Rules? Measuring How AI Coding Agents Escalate Authority in CI/CD Pipelines
papers.abstract: AI coding agents can modify CI/CD control-plane structures, including workflows and permission settings, thereby extending their authority beyond routine code changes. Because such modifications can affect an entire development pipeline, this study examines the trade-off between execution cost and governance risk in agentic CI/CD. We introduce a joint penalty model, P(M), that combines these two dimensions and evaluate it on all 932,791 agent-authored pull requests in the AIDev dataset, covering five autonomous coding agents. Each pull request is automatically classified by authority scope - data-plane or control-plane - and assigned a penalty score. We found that control-plane actions have a 2.3x higher mean joint penalty than data-plane actions (0.498 vs. 0.218) and a 3.9x higher mean governance risk (0.530 vs. 0.135), which means that they indeed increase the risk. All 775 pull reques

papers.title: Agent-Native Applications: A New Application Paradigm
papers.abstract: Traditional application architectures assume behavioral logic authored in advance, leaving reachable behavior largely bounded by explicit code and workflow rules. Large language model (LLM)-based agents challenge this assumption by enabling runtime reasoning and autonomous action to become part of application behavior, allowing applications to address situations not enumerated at design time. Extending this pattern, this paper identifies a new application paradigm in which LLM-based agents serve as central reasoning and action components responsible for the application's core logic and, where permitted, for adapting the application graph itself at runtime. We call these agent-native applications. While such applications significantly expand their possible behavioral space beyond explicit code and workflow rules, they also face a major control problem in which useful agentic reasoning sho

papers.title: Log Analysis for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
papers.abstract: Logs generated by LLM-based agents support analysis of execution behavior beyond final outputs. Existing surveys give limited attention to dependencies across the lifecycle of these records. A lifecycle-oriented review of 90 core studies published between 2024 and August 2026 covers Agent Logging, Agent Log Structuring, and Agent Log Mining. Stage-specific comparisons reveal cross-stage dependencies and limitations. Detailed logs do not necessarily provide sufficient evidence. Structural uniformity does not guarantee semantic equivalence. Analytical claims require alignment with supporting evidence, reference criteria, and validation procedures. Representative open-source tools, public datasets, and future research directions are also summarized.

papers.title: Keeping Up with the Kernel: Can LLMs Adapt Linux Drivers to Interface Changes?
papers.abstract: We analyze collateral evolution in Linux, the coordinated updates that drivers require when the kernel interfaces they depend on change, over the 20 years since it was first studied, covering releases from v3.0 to v7.2. Since v2.6.13, the number of driver files and support libraries has grown about eightfold, a single change to the most widely used library can now reach about 5.3k driver files, and such changes arrive either in bursts or spread over many releases. We introduce CoEvoBench, a benchmark that asks models to adapt an old driver module to a target kernel and evaluates the result against the developer's reference patch. The benchmark contains 316 manually confirmed tasks from 202 mainline commits and 268 modules, spanning kernel releases v6.19 to v7.2. It distinguishes 134 build-breaking tasks, where the old driver fails to compile, from 182 build-compatible tasks, where the ol

papers.title: Skill Roulette: Measuring Skill Invocation Rate Across LLM Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedures for large language model (LLM) coding agents. An agent selects a skill from its name and description before reading the procedure. It may complete the task without invoking a relevant skill. We investigate how reliably coding agents invoke relevant skills and which factors affect that decision. We estimate invocation rates by repeating trials with identical inputs; invocation rate is the proportion of trials in which the agent invokes the relevant skill. We test 9 non-directional hypotheses about skill metadata, competing skills, contextual instructions, and task wording and composition. Eight concern invocation; the ninth tests whether making a skill available changes the occurrence of an action that the task does not request. We use tasks from 4 software engineering categories in a synthetic repository, running each of 4 coding-agent harnesses with 2 mod

papers.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography Education for Software Developers: A Multivocal Literature Review
papers.abstract: Quantum computing threatens widely deployed public-key cryptography, making post-quantum cryptography (PQC) adoption a software engineering challenge. However, it remains unclear how well existing educational provision prepares software developers for secure PQC implementation and migration. We conducted a multivocal literature review of 8 research publications and 15 professional training offerings, examining competency coverage, practical software engineering tasks, pedagogical approaches, learner support, and evaluation. All 23 sources covered PQC foundations and algorithms, but coverage of practical software-engineering tasks was uneven. Our analysis identifies six gaps concerning developer focused evaluation, authentic software engineering tasks, task competency alignment, pedagogical design and learner support, security-focused assessment, and long term validation of learning outco

papers.title: f2x50: A Repository-Scale Benchmark for Fortran-to-X Software Migration
papers.abstract: Repository-level migration requires more than translating isolated functions: it must preserve behaviour across modules, shared state, build structure, and dependencies. Existing translation benchmarks predominantly cover small programs or small repositories, or fixed and widely studied language pairs. We present f2x50, a target-independent benchmark comprising 50 public Fortran repositories pinned to exact Git revisions. It contains 12,116 Git-tracked Fortran files and 6,569,806 lines, divided into three structural-complexity tiers and paired with 561 deterministic behavioural probes. Of these probes, 446 compile pinned source files with small drivers and span 131 repository--routine pairs. Every repository has at least five direct checks that collectively execute at least two routines. f2x50 provides target-independent tools for acquisition, validation, licence review, and reproducibil

papers.title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites
papers.abstract: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per sn

papers.title: ETA: Exit on Tool Arrival in Speculative Agent Loops
papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents in explicit thinking modes generate long chains of thought before acting, making each turn inherently serial: later tokens depend on the tool observation. Recent speculative tool dispatch methods overlap tool execution with reasoning, but offers limited benefit when reasoning dominates latency. We present ETA, that treats the speculative fork not as an actuator but as a sensor of the model's decision state, using it to terminate the reasoning of the main decode. It truncates reasoning only when the prediction is stable, agrees with the dispatched call, passes a free probe measuring whether a call will be emitted at all, and the tool result has arrived: a deadline that bounds per-turn regret by the remaining decode cost. ETA achieves speedups of 1.33x on tau2 airline/retail, 1.26x on tau2 telecom, and 1.13x on BFCL v4 multi-turn. On tau2, it decodes 24% fewer to

papers.title: The Limit Is in the Input, Not the Model: State-Dependent Command Safety in Natural-Language Interfaces to Industrial Controllers
papers.abstract: Language models judging commands to industrial controllers may not receive machine state, the equipment's current condition. The same command can require opposite safety decisions in different states, so an incorrect answer may reflect missing information rather than poor reasoning. We propose an answerability audit: does the model receive the information needed to decide? The audit records the model's inputs and pairs the same command with two states requiring opposite answers. The paired score counts a pair only when both answers are correct. We add rules, then state values, to the model's input. In an author-built test of 15 pairs from three systems with four language models, none reliably distinguished the paired cases without state, even with rules. With state, scores ranged from 0 to 13 correct pairs out of 15; three models improved. With text alone, one model always allowed comman

papers.title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. papers.title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
papers.abstract: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature spac

papers.title: Retroactive Concept Bottleneck Models for Exemplar-Free Class-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Exemplar-free class-incremental learning (EFCIL) requires models to learn new classes sequentially without retaining training samples from previous tasks. Continual concept bottleneck models (CBMs) make their predictions interpretable by identifying visual concepts in an image and using them to score each class. However, these methods typically focus on preserving learned concepts or approximating past classes with generated features, which can leave new concepts underused in old-class predictions. We propose RetroCBM, which retains a small set of vocabulary-independent statistics relating frozen visual features to the embedding space of a pretrained vision-language model. Even after earlier training images have been discarded, we can use these statistics to supervise new concepts. To do so, we develop a retroactive regression rule that yields the same predictor for each new concept as c

papers.title: Where Should a Diffusion Transformer Meet Its Teacher?
papers.abstract: Representation Alignment (REPA) significantly accelerates Diffusion Transformer training by guiding intermediate student features with a pretrained visual teacher, yet existing methods typically attach supervision to a single fixed layer. As student representations evolve, however, we find that the most effective layer for alignment varies across training stages. To track this evolving layer suitability online without costly search, we measure gradient compatibility between the flow-matching and alignment objectives, and propose AdaREPA, an online routing framework that adaptively selects the supervision layer as training progresses. AdaREPA uses a softmax distribution over smoothed layer compatibility scores to sample a layer for alignment at each training step. This probabilistic routing adapts teacher supervision to the student's changing learning needs, with minimal training overhead

papers.title: EgoJev: Finding Evidence in Egocentric Video by Reading VLM Decisions
papers.abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distrib

papers.title: Fuse Before Reconstruct: A Novel Reconstruction Paradigm for Multimodal Industrial Anomaly Detection
papers.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection plays a pivotal role in precision manufacturing, where joint analysis of multimodal data emerges as a critical approach to enhance detection accuracy. Feature reconstruction, a dominant paradigm for such joint analysis, is primarily implemented through intra-modal and cross-modal methods, both of which are plagued by significant limitations. Intra-modal reconstruction neglects complementary cross-modal information, while its cross-modal counterpart is prone to projection errors and ambiguous one-to-many mappings (e.g., same textures mapping to multiple geometries), leading to detection failures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel feature reconstruction paradigm, Fuse Before Reconstruct (FBR), which first fuses multimodal features and then performs reconstruction for anomaly detection. Firstly, we propose a bidirectional cross-modal attention mec

papers.title: Predicting Species Splits: A Challenging Fine-Grained Benchmark for Category Discovery
papers.abstract: Widely used category discovery benchmarks have become increasingly saturated and often fail to reflect real-world discovery settings, making long-term evaluation of new methods difficult. We introduce PS-SPLIT, a large-scale fine-grained benchmark for category discovery, motivated by taxonomic splitting: the real-world process by which what was once considered a single species is found to comprise multiple distinct ones. PS-SPLIT contains 79K globally distributed, high-quality, community-collected bird images spanning 771 species, derived from 257 recent real expert-verified taxonomic splits, with associated geographic metadata and full taxonomic hierarchy. The visual differences between categories arising from real taxonomic splits can be very subtle, often requiring significant human expertise to tell apart, making PS-SPLIT a challenging benchmark which we hope will assist in advancing

papers.title: ShoWorld: Shape-Faithful Multi-Hypothesis Occupancy World Model
papers.abstract: Occupancy world models struggle to forecast moving objects due to motion uncertainty and shape distortion. A single trajectory can average plausible futures into an implausible path, and repeated re-voxelization can erode or inflate object shape even under correct motion. We introduce ShoWorld to address these challenges through separate motion and shape representations. The motion forecaster predicts probabilistic trajectories conditioned on scene layout, nearby agents and the future ego trajectory. Each hypothesis is rendered into occupancy and fused according to its probability to retain alternative futures. The shape component predicts sub-voxel points with occupancy probabilities and offsets from local geometry. papers.title: SCOUT: Risk-Guided Foundation-Model Escalation for Robust Tissue Detection in Whole-Slide Images
papers.abstract: Reliable tissue detection is essential for whole-slide image analysis, yet high average segmentation accuracy can conceal failures involving pale tissue, small fragments, and heterogeneous staining. Pathology foundation models offer transferable representations, but exhaustive inference is computationally demanding and may introduce false-positive tissue predictions. We propose SCOUT (Selective Correction of Uncertain Tissue), a risk-guided cascade that selectively refines an initial thumbnail-based tissue mask. A lightweight audit network estimates the spatial distribution of segmentation errors and prioritizes candidate regions for processing by a frozen pathology foundation model. An asymmetric consensus rule integrates the resulting predictions with the initial mask to recover missed tissue while limiting false positives. papers.title: DORMS: Image Segmentation via Depth-Ordered Region Merge Trees
papers.abstract: We introduce DORMS (Depth-Ordered Region Merging for Segmentation), a purely algorithmic approach to image segmentation from monocular depth maps, requiring no neural networks or learned parameters in the segmentation process. An off-the-shelf monocular depth estimator provides the input depth maps. Our method constructs depth-ordered merge trees through a deterministic union-find sweep, combining component area, depth persistence, and spatial contact constraints to guide region merging. A threshold search determines the segmentation granularity according to a specified target region count, while global depth detrending improves the separation of local geometric structures. Extensive experiments on COCO Panoptic, Cityscapes, and ADE20K demonstrate consistent improvements over classical segmentation baselines and competitive performance against zero-shot neural segmentation models.
